articles.title: Nvidia’s DLSS 5, explained
articles.archive_body:
Nvidia knows that DLSS 5 left a bad first impression. In March, many gamers took one look at Resident Evil Requiem protagonist Grace Ashcroft’s DLSS 5-ified face and declared it AI slop. So this week, the company’s re-introducing its controversial “neural rendering” with firm messaging about how it “preserves artistic intent,” “respects the rendered frame,” and gives game developers full control.
Now, ahead of its September 3rd launch, with an official Nvidia briefing under our belt and some hands-on time with the version that leaked onto the web, we think we finally get the picture. Here’s what’s going on.
Is DLSS 5 AI slop?
The critics weren’t wrong: DLSS 5 largely is a generative AI filter for video games. Kind of like a camera filter on your phone, DLSS 5 analyzes and modifies a real-time stream of 2D images after your 3D game engine is done spitting them out. It can indeed make game characters look terrible if applied poorly, like they’ve aged 20 years in a split-second. It uses a lot of GPU power, and can easily cut framerate in half — even applied well, you could argue that existing games look better without it.
But DLSS 5 isn’t what we typically think of when we think of generative AI. It doesn’t change shapes, or hallucinate words on a sign, or place brand-new fake objects in view. Instead, it imagines light, shadow, color, and detail that make the same shapes appear differently.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/msedge_nJWTUL6t30.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
DLSS 5 can make dull, pasty characters look far more photorealistic. It can fill their hair and clothing and nearby foliage with signs of realistic light. It can ground characters and objects and clothing so they don’t look like they’re floating above video game surfaces.
Here’s an example I captured myself in Yakuza Kiwami: with DLSS on, see how contact shadows underneath each character make them seem like they’re actually standing on the ground?
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/YakuzaKiwami-2026-08-30-23-59-22_16.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/YakuzaKiwami-2026-08-30-23-59-22_15.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
(Later in this story, you should really check out how Steph Curry’s jersey casts shadows on his video game body, so it looks more like he’s wearing it.)
And unlike AI-generated photos and videos, that usually produce different results with the same prompt, Nvidia claims DLSS 5 is deterministic, so games should look the same every time.
DLSS 5 is also not one-size-fits-all. Despite what it sounds like, “DLSS 5 On” and “DLSS 5 Off” isn’t just an on-off switch. Developers (and apparently modders) can drag various sliders to change how DLSS 5 plays with color and light, and they have three different AI models to work with at launch, giving your graphics “default,” “natural” or “cinematic” looks.
Plus, developers can decide whether to apply DLSS 5 everything in a scene, just a character’s face and skin, just foliage, just silverware or furniture or even just food.
You’re saying game studios could leave character faces alone?
Yep. The toolset can automatically cut out a mask, like in Photoshop, to isolate a character’s face and skin from everything else:
[Image: The automated mask precisely selects this character’s face, so game developers can enhance it — or make sure it’s left alone. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/nvidia-dlss-5-010.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
If they don’t like the automated mask, devs can cut one out themselves. That’s the little “Developer Masking” checkbox in the image above. “There’s no limit to how many masks, how many groups, they could implement,” says Nvidia’s director of real-time content technology Gabriele Leone.
Would game studios actually leave the faces alone?
Probably not! The first game brave enough to ship with the tech is NBA 2K27, and I suspect that’s because Steph Curry actually looks a bit better with detailed skin, a uniform that doesn’t seem glued to his body, and a bit more glint in his eye. Take a look at Nvidia’s images for yourself:
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/assets_2026_08_1788195651_nba-2k27-nvidia-dlss-5-comparison-001-off.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/assets_2026_08_1788195651_nba-2k27-nvidia-dlss-5-comparison-001-on.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
That basketball, too — doesn’t it feel a bit more lifelike now most of its detail is in shadow?
But what about DLSStelle and all the other horrific AI faces I’ve seen since modders got hold of the tech?
[Media: https://bsky.app/profile/theswweet.myatproto.social/post/3mu6tsszqnk23]
Truly deranged. But these games are supposed to look like animation, and surely their creators would never do anything like this to them, right? Right??
“The soul and goal of GeForce is to achieve photorealism in real-time rendering,” Nvidia’s director of applied deep learning Edward Liu told journalists. And games with more realistic art styles don’t look anywhere near this bad. But even realistic games can look wrong if the sliders are set too aggressively.
What do you mean by “too aggressively?”
I’m willing to bet that if you’ve seen the leaked DLSS 5 modifying an existing game, the unofficial DLSS 5 mod was set to its default level of around 80 percent intensity or even higher. Some creators will even pump it up to 200 percent to make the difference between “DLSS on” and “DLSS off” especially clear.
But I believe even 80 percent is far too aggressive for many existing games. It can feel like you’re artificially aging a character by weathering their skin and deepening the wrinkles and creases in their face.
To show you, I fired up Shadow of the Tomb Raider. Here’s what Lara Croft looks like with DLSS 5 at 0 percent, 80 percent, and 200 percent intensity:
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/1-default-0.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/1-default-80.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/1-default-200.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
She seems… weathered, no? But at 40 percent intensity, she still looks like the same video game character to me, only with a bit more life in her eyes:
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/1-default-0.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/1-default-40.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Similarly, here’s Kazuma Kiryu from Yakuza Kiwami once more. In this part of the game, he’s supposed to be 27 years old, and nowhere near the grizzled veteran he is by Yakuza 6. But as I ramp up the intensity from 0 to 40 to 85 percent, you can see his furrowed brow gets more furrowed, his hair lightens, and the increased shadow across his cheeks makes his face appear slightly gaunt.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/YakuzaKiwami-1-0.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/YakuzaKiwami-1-40.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/YakuzaKiwami-1-85.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
He looks older — even if the underlying geometry of his face hasn’t actually changed. In a cutscene at 85 percent, it even looks like his hair might be tinged with grey:
[Image: Does this look like a 27-year-old man to you? https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/YakuzaKiwami-2026-08-31-00-15-21_57.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
But again, it’s something developers and modders can control with some granularity. I’d probably enjoy a version of DLSS 5 for older games that ignores the faces but enhances a character’s gear. Kiryu’s sworn brother and antagonist Nishiki, below, doesn’t quite look right to me — but his eyepatch and necklace look excellent.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/YakuzaKiwami-2026-08-31-00-14-19_44.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/YakuzaKiwami-2026-08-31-00-14-18_43.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
By the way, these are just me playing with the overarching DLSS 5 slider when set to its “default” model. There are actually three different AI models, each with a slightly different look, and two different sliders, one for “tone” and one for “structure.”
What’s the difference?
I’m telling myself that “tone” is about light and color, while “structure” is about shadows and definition. But it’s probably easier to show you by isolating each:
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/YakuzaKiwami-4-structure-0.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/YakuzaKiwami-3-tone-100_e64f6b.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/YakuzaKiwami-4-structure-100.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Officially, Nvidia says that “structure intensity” controls a mix of ambient occlusion, contact shadows, reflections and subsurface scattering (read: how light scatters through materials like hair, skin, and leaves), while “tone intensity” controls color and “broader lighting” details.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/msedge_nb8ulWaTDO.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
What about the three different AI models?
Nvidia only called them Model A, Model B and Model C in my briefing, but the DLSS 5 mod I used describes them as “default,” “cinematic” and “natural.” Here’s the image Nvidia provided to show the difference:
[Image: Nvidia’s three AI looks. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/nvidia-dlss-5-012.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
And here’s my own comparison in Shadow of the Tomb Raider — you may need to blow these up and cycle through to spot the differences.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/2-0-off.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/2-on-80.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/2-cinematic.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/2-natural.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Is this really an AI filter? It doesn’t use the game engine at all?
Nvidia says that DLSS 5 can take some cues from game engines. But it’s based on the colors and motion vectors that it sees in the flat 2D frames, after they’re rendered and after other techniques like DLSS Super Resolution are applied.
When we asked how DLSS 5 knows the difference between a character model, an object, and a piece of foliage, Liu replied that the model was trained to recognize what it sees. “Just like a person, if you look at anything, you know where things are.”
You can even technically run DLSS 5 on video capture from a Nintendo Switch 2, and modders have already found ways to inject it into earlier games that used OpenGL and DirectX 9.
Will game developers actually buy into DLSS 5? Will they use it well?
That’s one of the big remaining questions — and one that Nvidia left unanswered during and after our briefing.
While Nvidia said in March that DLSS 5 would come to at least 16 different games including Assassin’s Creed Shadows, Hogwarts Legacy, Starfield, and Resident Evil Requiem, the company did not answer questions about when DLSS 5 might come to any game beyond NBA 2K27, nor did it confirm that other titles are still coming following the original backlash. Perhaps Nvidia and its partners will wait and see how reviewers and gamers react first.
It’s worth noting that this may be a niche technology to start: while it no longer requires two RTX 5090 GPUs to function, it still uses a lot of horsepower. Officially, DLSS 5 is only coming to the latest RTX 50 series GPUs, which have become quite expensive: even a lower-mid-range RTX 5060 retailers for around $470 these days.
Nvidia claims that an RTX 5060 is enough to play NBA 2K27 at 1080p with ultra settings, ray tracing, and DLSS 5 enabled — assuming you’re pairing it with a fast gaming CPU and a whole heap of RAM.
[Image: These framerates are with 6x frame-gen enabled, so divide by six to get a better idea of how responsive the game might feel. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/nvidia-dlss-5-018.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Just how much of a performance hit are we talking?
With NBA 2K27, Nvidia claims the performance hit is 50 to 60 percent on average across all Nvidia RTX 50-series GPUs. When I ran the Shadow of the Tomb Raider benchmark at 1440p with on an RTX 5090 at Highest spec, DLSS Quality and an unofficial DLSS 5 mod, I saw framerate exactly cut in half — 312fps with DLSS 5 off, 156fps with it on.
Will gamers be able to tweak DLSS 5 the way they like?
The DLSS 5 mods are so easy to apply, it seems like the cat is out of the bag. But Nvidia’s message is that the developer has full control, and it didn’t answer questions about whether it’ll provide controls to gamers, too.
Which mod should I install?
I don’t yet feel comfortable recommending one — there’s been a feeding frenzy for DLSS 5 mods ever since the leak and we haven’t been able to properly vet. I installed one on a completely fresh system, just in case something went wrong.
How have gamers reacted to Nvidia’s re-introduction of DLSS 5 so far?
The reactions have been all over the place since DLSS 5 leaked and modders began posting their work. I’ve seen people say that DLSS 5 looks like a free next-gen remaster of any game you like, and I’ve seen people say it looks as terrible as it did before. I’ve seen people suggest that even if it looks good, it’ll make every game look too similar once developers start using it as a crutch.
But many of those impressions were based on images and videos of the tech at its extremes. Once people realize there’s granular control, perhaps reactions will become more measured.

articles.title: Here Are the Companies in Nvidia's $99 Billion Artificial Intelligence (AI) Portfolio. These 3 Are the Best of the Bunch
articles.body_method: publisher article-body, removing one identified stock-price widget; editorial and other contents preserved
articles.archive_body:
Most investors may not realize it, but venture capital funds, private equity firms, and investment banks are not the only institutions that buy stocks or support start-ups. Corporations can also buy stocks on the open market, and, from time to time, they make strategic investments in private companies.
At the close of
Nvidia
's
(
NVDA
-0.03%
)
fiscal second quarter, which ended July 26, the company boasted an investment portfolio totaling roughly $99 billion. Nvidia's investment book looks less like one of a stock-picker and more like a detailed map of the artificial intelligence (AI) supply chain.
The question is not whether
Jensen Huang
can pick winners. Spoiler alert: He can. The better questions to ask are which pockets of the AI ecosystem is Nvidia funding, and which of those opportunities are available to retail investors?
Let's break down Nvidia's investment strategy and assess what stocks and businesses the company owns that may be a fit for your portfolio, too.
Image source: Getty Images.
Where Nvidia is investing across the AI stack
The $99 billion in capital is spread across three buckets: publicly held stocks worth $47.7 billion, non-marketable securities worth $47.9 billion, and equity-method investments totaling $3.3 billion.
Public equities are split between listed common stock and a smaller layer of
convertible preferred stock
in public companies. According to Nvidia's
13F filing
, the biggest names in this category are
Intel
,
Space Exploration Technologies
, and
CoreWeave
(
CRWV
-0.15%
)
.
Nvidia invested $5 billion in Intel last September, while its SpaceX stock actually came from a check written for xAI after the two companies merged and then converted into a public holding. Meanwhile, Nvidia has invested in CoreWeave though multiple tranches over the last year.
During the second quarter earnings call, Nvidia CFO Colette Kress said the company has "invested nearly $50 billion in the frontier AI labs." The three names that matter most are OpenAI at $30 billion, Anthropic at up to $10 billion, and
Safe Superintelligence
at $5 billion.
The last bucket of investments revolves around stakes in infrastructure financiers as opposed to start-ups, frontier labs, and listed stocks. The one public name attached to this bucket is SB Energy, the
SoftBank
vehicle behind
OpenAI's Ohio campus
.
Of note,
Nvidia's acquisition of Hugging Face
for $12.9 billion is not included in this particular set of investments as the deal was announced after the quarter closed. Nvidia's capital is not sprinkled randomly; rather, it clusters in four core places.
First is the frontier labs. These companies are burning cash on compute faster than they can raise alternative financing like debt. So in this sense, Nvidia is becoming both a components supplier and a banker.
Second is the neocloud layer. CoreWeave and
Nebius
both build racks on Nvidia hardware and subsequently rent the capacity to developers who cannot get enough supply from the traditional hyperscalers --
Amazon
Web Services,
Microsoft
Azure, and Google Cloud Platform.
Third is the physical plumbing layer of the AI infrastructure stack. This is where photonics and optics sit, including Nvidia partners such as
Coherent
(
COHR
+4.16%
)
,
Lumentum
,
Marvell Technology
(
MRVL
+4.03%
)
, and
Nokia
.
Of note, Coherent shows up explicitly on Nvidia's 13F because the company's $2 billion investment went directly into common stock. Lumentum and Marvell do not follow the same structure. Each of these companies took $2 billion of convertible preferred, which is still public-company paper but is not listed common, so a 13F will not break it out until the preferred converts.
The fourth layer is a thin slice of applications and adjacent bets across biotech, robotics, and mobility through Nvidia's venture arm, NVentures. For now, these are
moonshots
, not the core of Nvidia's AI stack.
What Nvidia portfolio companies can retail investors buy?
Unfortunately,
retail investors
cannot directly buy OpenAI or the rest of Nvidia's private book. What they can buy are the public names Nvidia already owns: Intel, SpaceX, CoreWeave, Coherent, Nokia, Nebius, Lumentum, and Marvell.
In my eyes, the best of that bunch are CoreWeave, Coherent, and Marvell. CoreWeave is a direct proxy for the buildout of AI factories. The company owns GPUs and rents capacity to both hyperscalers and smaller developers, making it a direct beneficiary of the ongoing capital expenditure (capex) cycle. Coherent specializes in the optics bottleneck where dense chip clusters sit. Meanwhile, Marvell is the networking and silicon-photonics name Nvidia collaborated with to help integrate custom silicon into its fabric.
While buying Intel stock is tempting, shares have rallied hard since Nvidia's initial investment nearly a year ago. Meanwhile, SpaceX is still trying to prove its launch, satellite, and a broader AI ambitions can
scale enough to justify its trillion-dollar valuation
. Lastly, Nokia is more niche -- specializing in an AI-RAN for edge devices as opposed to core infrastructure across multiple platforms.
Ultimately, Coherent, CoreWeave, and Marvell line up nicely with the themes of rented compute, optical interconnects, and scale-up networking. These are established, usable applications within Nvidia's investment book that should fuel demand for more chips throughout the AI infrastructure era.

articles.title: NVIDIA, Microsoft Kick Off a New Beginning for Windows PCs with RTX Spark and AI Agents | NVIDIA Blog

articles.archive_body:
At a Microsoft event in San Francisco on Wednesday, Jensen Huang and Satya Nadella outlined how NVIDIA and Microsoft are co-engineering hardware and software for AI agents to run on Windows PCs.
NVIDIA was founded because of Windows, Huang said. Now AI agents are coming to Windows.
“If you look at the entire journey of our company, Windows was at the core of it,” Huang said, tracing back NVIDIA’s support for Windows and Microsoft over several decades. “If not for Windows there would be no GeForce.”
NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang connected that history — and his long-term vision — to the agentic era Wednesday during a fireside chat with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella hosted by Sriram Krishnan, a former senior White House policy advisor on AI at the Windows AI and Surface event, held at Dogpatch Studios in San Francisco.
“The thing that I really give Jensen all the credit for, quite frankly, is that consistency of vision of what this can be—not today, not tomorrow, but as a secular trend,” Nadella said. “And that’s what brings us to this moment.”
“The personal computer is the ultimate tool, it’s my ultimate tool, and for a whole generation of people, it’s our ultimate tool,” Huang said. “What happens in the era of agents, when the agent is on your computer? It is now your personal assistant.”
The event opened with Nadella before Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft’s EVP of Windows and Devices, walked through the Windows updates designed for the agentic era.
Turning Windows into a secure platform for agents, Microsoft announced general availability of Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), the OS-level infrastructure that lets agents run safely and persistently in the background, under operating system control.
“We are building these primitives directly into Windows, so agents can be secured, observed and governed,” Davuluri explained. “With MXC, Microsoft Security, and Agent 365, we’re unlocking the full potential of agents on Windows.”
Nadella returned to that theme in his talk with Huang. “We needed to make the desktop the most secure place for agents to execute,” Nadella said.
“What Satya just said is going to be the foundation of the next generation of IT as we know it,” Huang said. “Just as Windows and DirectX revolutionized how applications were built, MXC is going to revolutionize how agents are built and deployed.”
A New Beginning for Windows PCs: Preorder RTX Spark Laptops Today
Among the announcements Huang and Nadella outlined Wednesday, RTX Spark puts the full NVIDIA AI stack into Windows laptops and compact desktops, with laptop preorders open today and available October 16. Compact desktops will be available for sale in November.
Windows is bringing local AI closer to everyday work, while new hardware gives developers room to run increasingly capable models right on their PC. Introducing Surface Laptop Ultra, Pavan Davuluri tied that vision to NVIDIA RTX Spark.
“We built Surface Laptop Ultra around NVIDIA RTX Spark. With up to 128 gigs of unified memory and up to a petaflop of AI compute, you can run models on this laptop that simply don’t fit on a traditional machine,” Davuluri said.
Systems are coming from
Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft, MSI and Gigabyte
with designs ranging from slim laptops to compact desktops built for always-on agents.
RTX Spark combines an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with up to 6,144 cores, and an up to 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU connected at 600 GB/s.
One petaflop of FP4 AI performance and up to 128GB unified memory makes RTX Spark effective for local AI. It can run models such as Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, a 125B model with 51B n-gram that matches the intelligence of many cloud models, unmetered and without sending data to the cloud.
RTX Spark runs the full NVIDIA CUDA platform — the same software stack that runs across NVIDIA hardware — and is built for every way people use a PC:
Developers
can move models, tools and workflows without rewriting, running the same NVIDIA AI stack from RTX Spark to DGX Station.
Creators
get 5th-generation Tensor Cores with NVFP4 support, hardware-accelerated AV1, and 4:2:2 video encode and decode, DLSS and RTX ray tracing across the full production pipeline.
Gamers
can run AAA games at 1440p over 100 frames per second with DLSS 5, Reflex and G-SYNC.
The compact desktop configuration puts the same RTX Spark superchip in a small chassis designed for 24/7 operation — a dedicated local AI system that keeps agents running continuously.
Preorder RTX Spark today
.
NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows: Frontier AI Compute on the Enterprise Desktop
The event previewed NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows today — the first deskside AI supercomputer to bring GB300 Grace Blackwell-class AI infrastructure directly into the Windows ecosystem.
“This unlocks the power to run frontier-class models locally,”
Davuluri
said. “Capabilities that once required renting a cluster, now in a deskside supercomputer.”
Until now, DGX Station ran on Linux — which meant enterprise developers maintained two separate environments: Linux for heavy AI workloads and Windows for the productivity tools, applications and workflows.
The vast majority of Fortune 500 companies are standardized on Windows, and that gap has cost developers time and resources — developers either moved to Linux to access AI compute, or stayed in Windows with limited hardware options for heavy-duty model development and multi-agent workloads.
NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows runs on the GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra Desktop Superchip, delivering 748GB of coherent memory and up to 20 petaFLOPS of FP4 AI compute — enough to run models up to a trillion-parameter scale locally.
Teams of developers and researchers at AI-native companies, leading research labs and enterprises can build and run always-on AI agents that connect directly to the Windows applications and infrastructure they already use, and fine-tune and inference large models without leaving their primary machine. Linux AI toolchains remain accessible through WSL when needed.
Learn more about
NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows
and sign up to be the first to know when it’s available.
Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on
X
,
Instagram
,
TikTok
and
Facebook
— and stay informed by subscribing to the
NVIDIA Local AI newsletter
. Follow NVIDIA Workstation on
LinkedIn
and
X
.
See
notice
regarding software product information.
